newsitem.title: CHINA: FUND VIEW - HK re-rated as political discount fade.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - HK re-rated as political discount fade.

text.p: Bullish brokers and fund managers in Hong Kong are rushing to re-rate the world's sixth-largest stock exchange just a few weeks after the former British colony returned to Chinese rule.
"The political discount is gone and it has turned into a China premium," said Tina So, director at Schroders Investment Management.
"The broad picture is positive and the Hong Kong market is still undervalued against its long-term potential."

Brokers had upgraded their end-1997 targets for Hong Kong's blue-chip Hang Seng index, spurred by optimism about Hong Kong's growing exposure to a stable Chinese economy, a benign U.S. interest rate environment and continued liquidity inflows, both from China and overseas.

Goldman Sachs last week upgraded an end-1997 Hang Seng forecast to 17,288 from 15,800. Merrill Lynch had already revised upwards its end-1997 Hang Seng target to 18,000 and believes the index could rise to 19,000 within 12 months.
Many fund managers in Hong Kong have followed suit. Prudential Asia now holds a target of 18,000 by end-1997 while Schroders forecasts a rise to 18,500 over the same period.

The upgrades imply a multiple of 15 times 1998 earnings against 13 times 1997 earnings at the beginning of the year, suggesting rising confidence in Hong Kong's future now that the July 1 transition to Chinese sovereignty has passed.
Earlier this year Hong Kong lagged index multiples on stock markets throughout the region, which were all trading above 15 times with the exception of Thailand and the Philippines.
Even Taiwan, with its complex political landscape, has been trading at more than 30 times 1997 earnings.
"There were special risks associated with Hong Kong," said David Descalzi, senior portfolio manager at Prudential Asia.
"But the more the mainland helps itself in the way it administers this region and the more people feel comfortable that the transition has occurred successfully, that will assist the re-rating."

The Hang Seng's continued reach into record territory indicates the end of investor caution and a rush to gain access to the China growth story through closer economic ties between Hong Kong and China.
"A lot of the major traditional hongs (trading houses) in Hong Kong are broadening their business base in China, striking strategic alliances," Schroders' So said.

"We have long been arguing that Cheung Kong should not be looked at as a property play. After this restructuring it is clear they are positioning themselves as a major (company) in China markets. Yet these guys are trading at nine times earnings, and that's just one example."
Hong Kong's blue chip laggards are not only catching up with the rest of the region, they are closing the gap with Hong Kong's red hot red chip sector.
Many stocks among this expanding mass of China-related companies with mainland financial backing are trading in excess of 40 times 1997 earnings.
The overall re-rating of the Hong Kong stock market had been helped by the red chips as mainland parents exploit the market to realise value, said Descalzi.
But he views this "reddening" process as a mixed blessing. The influence of economic fundamentals has declined, causing an increase in market volatility.
"The market is becoming more and more local," he said. "It's not that the fundamentals aren't there, it's that what is driving it is not fundamental, and that is a concern."
This makes the market harder to read, and it also signals a change in corporate culture.
"As mainland companies infiltrate Hong Kong companies, they will bring their own special way of doing business which may jeopardise minority stakeholders," he said.
